We thank the reviewer for their thoughtful review. We address their comments below.

## Assumptions on user visibility (W1, W2 and Q1)

> Q1: Can MURMUR be easily extended to remove the two assumptions mentioned in W1 and W2?

We would like to clarify that the assumption "users only see messages corresponding to their own tasks" is not a fundamental assumption of the MURMUR framework itself, but rather an experimental setting choice for our simulated user agents. We implemented this setting simply to get a cleaner, more stable simulation of user behavior, as otherwise the user agents get confused on their tasks and start responding unpredictably.

To prove this point, we ran a new experiment where we removed this constraint and allowed simulated users to see all cross-talk. These results are for 5 concurrent tasks at a time, with varying number of users per task

Results on GPT-4.1

| Domain    | TSR     | TSR (cross talk) | ASR     | ASR (cross talk) |
|-----------|---------|------------------|---------|-------------------|
| Airline   | 43.6%  | 14.0%            | 66.68%  | 68.31%            |
| Slack     | 71.4%   | 61.2%            | 44.76%  | 45.86%            |
| Workspace | 70.4%   | 54.6%            | 33.33%  | 35.12%            |


Thus, in the simulations, making the user agents see cross-talk only degrades utility (and the degradation is much higher for complex benchmarks like Airline). The ASR still remains very high.

We will explicitly state this distinction between the framework and the experimental setting in the revised paper.

## Grouping function vs defenses (W3 and Q2)

> W3: It is unclear how these two grouping operations (the grouping function in Section 4.1 and the task-based clustering defense) differ or relate to each other.

The mapping function $g$ mentioned in Section 4.1 is part of the problem setup; it represents the “ground truth” grouping of users to tasks, which is unknown to the agent. If the agent were aware of this mapping, the problem of multi-user collaborative agents could be easily solved!

The task-based clustering in Section 6 is the defense that works precisely because the agent doesn't know g, and it is the agent's attempt to reconstruct this mapping by dynamically clustering users.

We will improve the clarity of the ground truth and the defense’s estimation in the revised paper.

## Related work (W4)

Thank you for the excellent reference, which we will add to our related work section. Notably, the threat model of CUP and the Cross-domain Context Bypass (C6) in [a] are fundamentally different: 
Our CUP attack identifies a vulnerability in single-agent, multi-user settings, where an agent with full visibility of a shared transcript fails to attribute instructions. While C6 targets federated, multi-agent systems, where context is fragmented across different agents, and the vulnerability arises when a user queries these separate agents and combines their partial, benign responses to reconstruct confidential information. Thus, C6 exploits an external combination of fragmented contexts, while CUP exploits an agent's internal failure to disentangle a single, shared context.

## Clarifying the threat model (single-user jailbreak vs multi-user poisoning)

> Competing hypothesis for success of CUP

Thank you for your insightful review. You are correct that the scenarios you propose would also be multi-turn attacks. However, the threat model is fundamentally different.

The scenarios you propose are single-user, multi-turn direct prompt injections (DPI). In this setting, the attacker's objective is to make the model do something for themselves. The attacker is, in effect, only “attacking themselves”. While in our work, the attacker’s goal is to poison the agent’s shared context to attack other benign users. This objective is similar to indirect prompt injections (IPI), but IPIs are often blocked by existing defenses, which is precisely why this new multi-user attack vector is so significant (easier to affect others, harder to defend against).

> The agent knows who made the request to include the phishing link. Rather, the agent fails because it does not recognize the request as malicious, which is the same failure mode as in the traditional jailbreaking.

We agree this is part of the failure, but the multi-user setting introduces a deeper vulnerability. To be useful, a collaborative agent must be able to take a helpful instruction from one user and apply it to others. The core failure we highlight is the agent’s inability to distinguish which instructions should apply to which users. To clarify this, the instruction does not need to be obviously malicious like a jailbreaking instruction. A benign-looking rule might be helpful for one user but undesirable to another. This is a failure of attribution and application, not just malicious content detection. 

Figure 1 in the paper makes a direct comparison between IPI and CUP using an obviously malicious instruction. Below is a new example of Continua which shows the model’s inability to selectively apply the rule to the intended users, and it is different from jailbreaks.

Continua is a real-world multi-user agent, it is aware of the different users interacting and what roles they have in a discord server.

**Continued in next comment**

Thank you for the follow-up. We appreciate the opportunity to clarify this distinction, as it is central to the paper's contribution.

The analogy with a public Google Doc fits passive attacks (IPI): the agent reads external content that might be edited by untrusted parties. But even for IPI, we would not call this a “fundamental limitation of collaborative spaces/untrusted sources unrelated to AI”, since there are already well-studied mitigations. CUP is different because a user actively changes the agent’s policy/behavior. And because there’s no clear separation between data and instruction during the collaborative conversation, existing IPI defenses fail to enforce the boundaries. Addressing CUP, therefore, requires system-level authority scoping plus the model’s inherent social intelligence to track who a preference or rule applies to.

To explain this point, we present a non-malicious conversation we just had with Continua.

**Bob — 1:21 PM**
@Continua please respond in Chinese! I cant read any other language

**Continua
APP
 — 1:21 PM**
好的，从现在开始我会用中文回复您。

**Krimo — 1:21 PM**
@Continua whats the date today

**Continua
APP
 — 1:21 PM**
今天是2025年11月26日，星期三。

Currently, there is no malicious input from any user. There is no jailbreak as such. Yet, the model applies Bob's preferences to those of Krimo. Thus, we believe that this issue fundamentally stems from the incorrect attribution of preferences to the correct users.

**Edit**: Interestingly, continua's first reply says "好的，从现在开始我会用中文回复您:" i.e.  "Okay, from now on I will reply to you in Chinese.", yet it replies to Krimo too in Chinese, which clearly shows the discrepancy we are talking about!

Again, to cause something truly malicious, some manipulations and jailbreaks will need to be applied; however, the fact that they transfer so easily to other users is our key observation. Otherwise, even Indirect Prompt Injections are an instantiation of jailbreaks; it is the inability of the LLMs to detect harmful requests in their context! The fact that these harmful requests come from external data sources, not provided by the original user, is what makes the attack vector interesting to study.

In our case, it is akin to a public shared computer with a very clear separation between the containers that different users have, and yet user A is still able to influence what happens to user B. It turns out that this happens due to vulnerabilities in the internal operating system, which is that the operating system itself cannot really distinguish between different users, and the separation is only in the frontend and what is displayed to the users. The fact that jailbreaks can cause issues in these settings, where attacks can spread to other users, is due to this lack of inherent separation.

### On the validity of the scenarios

Although the crypto example is unusual, it is true. ElizaOS is an immensely popular bot used by individuals to analyze the sentiment of cryptocurrencies on Twitter and automatically execute trades and buy cryptocurrency. It has a transfer function that allows the main user to withdraw from their account or send to any other account. However, internally, there is no such separation as to who can call what tools in ElizaOS's implementation, which allows an external user to place such bizarre-looking requests. 

This is the standard architecture for modern agentic deployments in group settings right now. Discord bots (like Midjourney or moderation bots), Slack apps, and Customer Service agents operate in semi-public shared channels with privileged tools (banning users, issuing refunds, accessing calendars). As these agents move from simple command-line interfaces to LLM-driven semantic reasoning (the industry trend), they inherit the CUP vulnerability. A bot that can "ban users" is useful; a bot that is tricked into banning the admin because a user redefined the definition of "spam" in the shared context is the specific failure mode MURMUR investigates.

summary.value: This paper proposes a cross-user poisoning (CUP) attack targeting multi-user agentic collaboration scenarios. The CUP attack exploits the inability of LLM agents to distinguish instructions from different users within a shared session, injecting seemingly benign malicious instructions into the shared context to compromise other users' tasks. The authors also introduce a benchmark framework named MURMUR to systematically observe the consequences of CUP and evaluate the performance of LLM agents under this threat.

strengths.value:
S1. This paper identifies a significant threat in multi-user agentic collaboration scenarios.

S2. The proposed benchmark framework is well defined mathematically.

S3. Through experimental analysis, the authors identify the fundamental reason behind the success of CUP attacks as the LLM agents' difficulty in disentangling contexts.

weaknesses.value:
W1. MURMUR assumes that users only see messages corresponding to their own tasks. The authors justify this assumption by arguing that real humans also ignore messages from unrelated users and isolate the necessary context for themselves. However, in real-world scenarios, a small portion of users may still attend to unrelated messages addressed to them. Completely disregarding the existence of such users may undermine the reliability of the simulation results.

W2. Similarly, MURMUR assumes that users only see the per-group view and are not influenced in their interactions by cross-talk. However, in the real world, a small subset of users may not conform to this assumption.

W3. I cannot fully understand the task-based clustering defense strategy proposed in Section 6. This strategy dynamically clusters users into different task groups to restrict their context access. However, in Section 4.1, the authors have already assumed that users are assigned to different task groups by a mapping function g. It is unclear how these two grouping operations differ or relate to each other.

W4. The following paper [a] proposes a security challenge named Cross-domain Context Bypass (C6), which appears to be similar to the CUP attack. I believe this paper should discuss the differences and connections between these two threats.

[a] Seven Security Challenges That Must be Solved in Cross-domain Multi-agent LLM Systems.

For Figure 6a), we agree that, although the difference in values is small, the trend is clear and consistently points downwards, especially from 2 simultaneous tasks to 5 simultaneous tasks.

For 6b), we have plotted the 95% confidence interval for the population mean. Since it is not a binary yes/no value and involves averaging across different benchmarks, plotting the 95% CI of the actual values of tool calls would not have resulted in meaningful results for us. 

However, we add some additional statistics corresponding to Figure 6b here, especially for the airline domain, which displayed the most variation in values (the highest mean standard error), and the domain where benign utility is the least.

Average number of messages per task (between user and agent)

| # Tasks | Average Number of messages | stddev |
|---|---|---|
| 1| 8.26 | 7.35 |
| 2| 23.60 | 10.23 |
| 3| 13.52 | 17.12 |
| 4| 24.44 | 9.15 |
| 5| 40.18 | 92.43 |

We observed that a few tasks (~6%) exceeded the maximum number of back-and-forth interactions allowed between the user and the agent when running five tasks simultaneously. We had allowed a maximum of 100 * number of simultaneous tasks, or 3.3 times the allowance in Tau-Bench. This does not happen with a smaller number of simultaneous tasks. Furthermore, the average values we report above are *excluding* the tool call counts from the tasks that exceed the limit (as those tasks are incomplete). Similarly, the tool call statistics do not include the values for these tasks.

This allows us to claim that there is at least some amount of confusion that creeps in for the agent, causing it to use a significantly greater number of messages to solve the same task.

summary.value: The paper introduces cross-user poisoning (CUP)—a new attack vector unique to multi-user LLM agents that operate in shared workspaces (e.g., Slack/Discord). In CUP, an attacker posts seemingly legitimate instructions that become part of the persistent shared state, causing the agent to later execute the attacker’s intent while serving benign users. The authors show CUP succeeds on popular multi-user agents in the wild and persists across tasks—unlike classic prompt injection that targets untrusted data sources rather than other users’ instructions. They then propose MURMUR, a framework that uplifts single-user tasks into concurrent, persona-driven multi-user scenarios to stress-test agents for CUP; they report high attack success and long-lived propagation, and explore a first-step defense via task-based clustering to contain cross-task leakage.

strengths.value:
+ The paper crisply distinguishes CUP from both direct and indirect prompt injection by highlighting the user-vs-user instruction conflict.

+ The authors successfully attack two deployed multi-user agents (Continua, ElizaOS), including a step-by-step demonstration where an instruction persists and later triggers a malicious reminder link;

weaknesses.value:
- I cannot find the practicality for the proposed attack as shown in Figure 2. To me, this is just another malicious user's prompt instruction, and the LLM follows it. I acknowledge the story is interesting, but the threat model is unclear. Why does a user do this in a collaborative environment? Suspicious behaviors can be easily found by others. Have you done a user study?

- Experiments span three adapted environments and four model backends; however, the landscape of multi-user agent deployments is broader (productivity suites, CRM, code-assist in chat). The narrow environment sets risks of overfitting conclusions to chosen tool APIs and dialog dynamics. 

- The defense focuses on containment via clustering; the paper acknowledges that in-cluster attacks remain unsolved and clustering accuracy is a linchpin.

questions.value:
1. Beyond containment, what mechanisms (e.g., per-user provenance tags, signed-instruction checks, scoped memories) best mitigate in-cluster CUP, where attackers are part of the same task? Any preliminary results?

2. How do ASR/APR curves shift with attacker budget  B, different interleavings (front-loaded vs. late attacks), or stealth (short, policy-like phrases vs. verbose templates)?

3. Since users do not see tool traces but the agent does, how much of the persistence is due to tool-trace conditioning vs. message history alone? Can filtering/siloing tool traces reduce persistence without large TSR drops?

title.value: Summarization Comment for the Area Chair

comment.value:
Dear Area Chair,

We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful evaluations. Across reviewers, our work was consistently recognized for identifying a new and important vulnerability in multi-user LLM agents, providing rigorous mathematical formalization, and demonstrating real-world impact through successful attacks on deployed systems.

**Key strengths highlighted by reviewers:**

1. **Novel Vulnerability Identification (Reviewers NWdc, Xu6N, dvZ8):**  
CUP exposes a previously unexamined failure mode: cross-user propagation of instructions due to insufficient user-specific scoping, which is distinct from both direct and indirect prompt injection. Reviewers emphasized its importance as multi-user deployments rapidly grow.

2. **Strong Real-World Validation (Reviewers Xu6N, dvZ8):**  
Our attacks on *Continua* and *ElizaOS* demonstrate long-lived policy injections, cross-platform propagation (including cryptocurrency redirection), and incorrect transfer of even benign preferences across users. Reviewer dvZ8 found these examples “especially compelling.”

3. **Mathematical Clarity and Formalism (Reviewers NWdc, Xu6N):**  
Reviewers highlighted the precision of our multi-user interaction model, shared-state formalization, and clear decomposition of task-dependent and attacker-dependent behaviors.

4. **General and Scalable Framework (Reviewers NWdc, Xu6N):**  
MURMUR was viewed as a clean, extensible benchmark that systematically lifts single-user tasks (from Tau-Bench and AgentDojo) into multi-user concurrent settings without overfitting to a specific environment.

5. **Comprehensive Empirical Findings (Reviewers NWdc, Xu6N):**  
CUP achieves high ASR across Slack, Workspace, and Airline domains; exhibits strong persistence across tasks; and remains effective despite modern PI defenses—highlighting a qualitatively different threat vector.

6. **Meaningful First-Step Defense (Reviewers NWdc, Xu6N):**  
Task-based clustering eliminates cross-task transfer (ASR → 0) while maintaining within-task utility, surfacing realistic trade-offs for future defenses.

---

**Summary of revisions and reviewer concern resolution:**

**Resolution of Conceptual Concerns:**  
Reviewer dvZ8 was initially skeptical and questioned whether CUP reduced to multi-turn jailbreaking. After our demonstrations showed even benign user preferences propagating incorrectly (e.g., language preferences), as well as failures in real-world agents like Continua, the reviewer explicitly stated that their conceptual concerns were *resolved* and emphasized the importance of surfacing such vulnerabilities in widely deployed agents.

**New Experiments:**

- **Cross-talk ablation (NWdc):** Removing visibility restrictions yields sharply lower TSR but ASR remains high, showing the assumption was not fundamental.  
- **Confidence intervals and statistical rigor (dvZ8):** 666-run re-evaluation with CIs added; claims updated accordingly.  
- **Attacker budget & tool-trace filtering (Xu6N):** More injections slightly increase persistence; filtering tool traces reduces utility but does *not* mitigate CUP, clarifying persistence mechanisms.

**Clarifications to Methodology and Threat Model:**

- Clear distinction between ground-truth grouping \( g \) and the clustering-based defense.  
- Revised terminology to avoid ambiguity around “attribution,” now explicitly describing failure to selectively apply rules only to the requesting user.  
- Expanded threat-model discussion on anonymity, message deletion, and cross-platform state in real systems.

summary.value:
The paper investigates the security of language model (LM) agents operating in a setup where they serve multiple users and have shared memory. The paper suggests that such agents are vulnerable to a specific type of attack, where a malicious actor "plants" the instructions into the memory of the LM, such that these instructions are only executed at a later time point, when the LM is operating on behalf of another user. The paper poses that such delayed execution is not covered by the standard prompt injection framework and thus remains an open vulnerability.

To study this issue and propose remedies, the paper introduces MURMUR, a multiagent interaction framework where the agent, the users, and the attacker are simulated by LMs. MURMUR setups adapt single-user agentic tasks from other benchmarks (Tau-bench and AgentDojo) into the desired form. The paper then investigates the success rate of the planted cross-user attacks. It finds that the agents are highly susceptible to such attacks and that the malicious instructions persists strongly as the agent continues to work on future tasks. Furthermore, traditional prompt injections are found to not be as effective. The paper also finds that shared context, until a certain number of concurrent users, is beneficial to the agents for successful and more efficient completion of user requests. Finally, the paper proposes a mitigation of the cross-user attacks based on limiting the context of the agent when attending to individual users. This mitigation is shown to drive the ASR to zero across all studied domains.

strengths.value:
- The setting of an agent serving multiple users with shared memory is highly relevant. Clearly, such agents will be deployed more broadly, and security vulnerabilities will be more critical when one attacker can "poison" the agent so that many other users are harmed.
- The paper provides examples of subverting real LLM-based agents Continua and ElizaOS. The case of having the agent move cryptocurrency to a wrong address when poisoned across platforms (in Appendix B) is especially compelling.
- MURMUR framework allows incorporation of existing single-user benchmarks, making it more scalable.

weaknesses.value:
## Competing hypotheses for success of CUP
My main concern with the paper is that it is not clear to me that the attacks it proposes necessarily succeed because of the setup being _multi-user_. In my understanding, from the results of the paper, two natural competing hypotheses cannot be refuted, namely that the attacks succeed because they are _multi-turn_ or because the prompt injections used in the paper are better than the outdated baselines. Below I discuss these hypotheses in more detail.

1. The results might stem from the attack being _multi-turn_. In L77-79, it is written about Fig. 1 (emphasis mine):
> However, in a multi-user environment (the right panel), a malicious instruction can be established as a persistent rule under the guise of a helpful policy. As a result, the agent, unable to **attribute** the persistent rule solely to the attacker, incorrectly applies it to benign users. 

In my understanding, attribution is not an issue in the example in Figure 1. The agent knows who made the request to include the phishing link. Rather, the agent fails because it does not recognize the request as malicious, which is the same failure mode as in the traditional jailbreaking. To see that having multiple users is crucial, a useful ablation would be to have Mallory (the attacker) to set the reminders for Carlos and Dana. This way, the multi-turn structure of the dialogue would be preserved, with all the cluttering context that could prevent the agent from seeing the malicious intent, while the multi-user aspect of it would be removed. Looking at the example attack in Appendix G, I have the same concern. In the example, the attacker (Jason Yu) sets up the environment such that the agent will later execute the actions of sending malicious emails. Then, a benign user (Ryan Lee) requests an unrelated task and the agent sends the emails before executing the task. What would've happened if Jason Yu himself requested this unrelated task?

2. An even simpler hypothesis could be that the large ASR comes from a newer prompt injection template. The paper compares cross-user poisoning (CUP) attacks against prompt injections in Table 3. However, from L449-450, I get the impression that the original prompt injections from AgentDojo have been used. If that is the case, of course the LLMs that have been introduced after AgentDojo would incorporate defenses (all of the LLMs in table 3 have been released after AgentDojo). Thus, the PI baseline in Table 3 seems inadequate. Instead, some variation of the template used for CUP (Figure 8 in the Appendix) should be tried for a single-step attack as well.


## Statistical significance
I also suspect that the results in the paper might be statistically underpowered. In particular, Figure 6 reports the success of GPT-4.1 as the agent when varying the number of tasks it does concurrently. In my understanding, these were generated from a total of 111 tasks. The 95% Wilson interval for the first number on the left (approx. 66%) would then be approx. [57%, 74%]. This includes more than the entire y-axis range of the plot. I suspect that similar underpowering is happening with the tool call count averaging. Taking this into account, I cannot currently trust the discussion in Section 5.3.

To confirm or reject this concern, it would be useful to see confidence intervals reported for at least some of the results in the paper.

## The defense
I think the defense proposed in the paper is overfitted to the particular design choices of MURMUR and cannot be applied in a scalable way. The whole point of multi-user collaboration with an agent is that the users can influence the agent in a way that propagates to everyone else. The example in Fig. 1 right could also have been a benign interaction, where Mallory just notifies the agent about the (legitimate) website of the workshop. In that case, this information should be correctly propagated by the agent to others in the reminders. If I understand it correctly, the groups-based defense proposed in Section 6 would make such an interaction impossible. Correspondingly, the reason why TSR doesn't change strongly in Table 4 with the defense is that the tasks that the users request are mostly isolated (indeed, they were adapted from _single-user_ benchmarks), hence the shared memory, a key element of the MURMUR setup, is actually barely useful to the agent.

The defense also looks like it could be compromised if one targets the "lightweight classifier" assigning agents to groups.

## Minor points
- Fig. 5 is counterintuitive / borderline misleading. The text does mention that this is _conditioned on at least one task being compromised_, and the caption should too. From a cursory glance it reads as if the first task is just always compromised by the attack vector in question.
- The proposed defense and results should not be in the Discussion section but rather stand as its own section or incorporated into the previous section.
 
- L449: missing number for PI success

questions.value: Why does the user only see the messages corresponding to their task (L249)? It looks like the discord agent, for example, is added to a specific channel and all interactions with it are public. I think this might actually be an issue if the attacker has to put their prompt injection into the shared channel for everyone to see.

comment.value:
## Practicality of the attack (W1)

> the threat model is unclear. Why does a user do this in a collaborative environment? Suspicious behaviors can be easily found by others.

Thank you for your feedback. We argue that this attack is highly practical.

Our threat model is applicable to any collaborative environment, where the attacker’s goal is to poison the agent’s shared context to attack other benign users. We demonstrated this practicality by successfully attacking two real-world agents, Continua and ElizaOS.

Regarding traceability: In a large, permissionless, and anonymous setting (like a public Discord or Slack), an attacker can easily post the malicious instruction and leave the group or delete messages, which still stay in the context of these chatbots. Similarly, ElizaOS analyzes the sentiment of cryptocurrencies on Twitter and automatically executes trades and buys cryptocurrency, while also interacting with public accounts. It is impossible to track the multitude of accounts on Twitter in a multi-user setting like this. In terms of user study, post submission to ICLR, we are having discussions with Continua regarding this threat vector, which is aware of problems like this from their analysis of the domain:  https://blog.continua.ai/p/agentifying-the-group-chat

## Environment breadth (W2)

> The narrow environment sets risks of overfitting conclusions to chosen tool APIs and dialog dynamics.

First we would like to highlight that the vulnerability is not tied to a specific application but is agnostic to the context. It stems from the fundamental interaction model of a single agent serving multiple users in a shared context.
Our intent in adapting tasks from different benchmarks (Tau-bench, AgentDojo) was to demonstrate that the CUP vulnerability is general and not an artifact of one type of task. We agree that exploring its effects in even broader, more diverse environments is a valuable direction for future work, and we will add this to our discussion.

## In-cluster defense (W3 and Q1)

We agree. As we state in our limitations (L477-481), our proposed defense is a first step focused on containment, and we explicitly acknowledge that in-cluster attacks remain an open problem and a key area for future research. Mitigating in-cluster attacks may require fundamentally new mechanisms from both system design (like scoped memory as the reviewer suggested) and improvements in model’s capabilities (like social intelligence).  

## ASR curves with different budgets and tool traces (Q5, Q6)

We experimented with GPT-4.1 with 5 concurrent tasks and varied the attacker budget, to have an attacker message randomly inserted into the conversation 1 and 2 times along with the initial injection. We observed that it increased attack persistence and led the model to remember performing the injection.

Results for GPT-4.1 with ≥5 injections across domains.

| Domain    | 0  | 1  | 2  |
|-----------|----|----|----|
| Slack     | 4  | 7  | 9  |
| Workspace | 9  | 13 | 15 |
| Airline   | 8  | 12 | 14 |

There was not a significant difference in Persistence but a slight reduction in TSR on removing tool traces with GPT4.1 

| Domain    | TSR     | TSR (tool filter) | ≥5 Persistence | ≥5 Persistence (tool filter) |
|-----------|---------|--------------------|----------------|------------------------------|
| Airline   | 43.6%  | 39.4%             | 4              | 3                            |
| Slack     | 71.4%   | 69.8%              | 9              | 10                           |
| Workspace | 70.4%   | 64.3%              | 8              | 8                            |

Thus, solely removing tool traces is not enough to defend the model but is essential for more utility.

I appreciate that the authors have now added confidence intervals to their plots. I believe that my concern with Figure 6 (a) was correct. With the confidence intervals, _all of the values for num. tasks from 2 to 5 are within the CI for the value from task 1_! The null-hypothesis that there is no dependence on the number of tasks cannot be rejected. I would not make any conclusions from this plot.

I'm also confused as to how did the authors provide the CI for Figure 6 (b). I'm highly doubtful that this kind of confidence can be achieved, especially given the CI on Figure 6 (a). Could the authors please provide the methodology? It would also be nice to add the methodology for CIs to the figure/table captions.

Could you please explain how you computed the 95% CI for the population mean in this case? I can imagine multiple approaches here. What was the sample size when computing the mean? If I understand correctly and Table 10 references this, I imagine it was around 400, in which case you should definitely not get such narrow intervals.

Edit: from the additional statistics table in the response, it also seems that Fig. 6 (b) is strongly underpowered and no conclusions can be made as to the trend of these averages, like with Fig. 6 (a)

## Defense

> If I understand it correctly, the groups-based defense proposed in Section 6 would make such an interaction impossible.

We agree with your assessment and were transparent about this in the paper (L477-481). We position this clustering defense as a “first step” that explicitly makes a trade-off between security and utility: It intentionally restricts benign cross-task collaboration (utility) to contain the attack’s impact within a single cluster (security). 

> hence the shared memory, a key element of the MURMUR setup, is actually barely useful to the agent.

This is not true. Our defense only affects cross-task collaboration, The shared memory remains essential for multi-user in-task collaboration, which is the core of our setup. Users solving the same tasks need the agent to classify them as solving the same tasks well in order to get a good task success rate.

> The defense also looks like it could be compromised if one targets the "lightweight classifier" assigning agents to groups.

Even if an attacker tricks the classifier into placing them in the wrong group, the attack's impact is still limited to that single cluster. It does not propagate to all users, thus still achieving its containment goal. But yes, we acknowledge this as a caveat of the current defense (line 479 in the original paper).

## Minor points

Thank you for your rigorous review, we will fix the caption on Figure 5 to state it is conditioned, move the defense to the experiments section and add the missing number for PI success.

> Why does the user only see the messages corresponding to their task (L249)?

We would like to clarify that the assumption "users only see messages corresponding to their own tasks" is not a fundamental assumption of the MURMUR framework itself, but rather an experimental setting choice for our simulated user agents. We implemented this setting simply to get a cleaner, more stable simulation of user behavior.

To prove this point, we ran a new experiment where we removed this constraint and allowed simulated users to see all cross-talk.

Results on GPT-4.1

| Domain    | TSR     | TSR (cross talk) | ASR     | ASR (cross talk) |
|-----------|---------|------------------|---------|-------------------|
| Airline   | 43.6%  | 14.0%            | 66.68%  | 68.31%            |
| Slack     | 71.4%   | 61.2%            | 44.76%  | 45.86%            |
| Workspace | 70.4%   | 54.6%            | 33.33%  | 35.12%            |

Thus, in the simulations, making the user agents see cross-talk only degrades utility (and the degradation is much higher for complex benchmarks like Airline). The ASR still remains very high.

We will explicitly state this distinction between the framework and the experimental setting in the revised paper.

- However, now, as mentioned above, when Mallory asks it not to stop replying even if someone asks it to, it refuses to listen to Krimo, despite being the admin. Explicitly telling the model that Mallory is a spammer does not work either, and the model continues to respond to how Mallory asked, because Mallory instructed it to do so. This differs from a jailbreak, where an input attempts to bypass constraints that are typically applied. In our case, the model is not able to distinguish between the preferences of different users, even though both preferences are valid in their contexts.

Continua itself mentions this problem while coming up with their solution for group conversations with LLMs: https://blog.continua.ai/p/agentifying-the-group-chat. However, it looks like they still have not landed on a perfect solution for this issue, as evidenced by our successful attacks.

We will add images of these conversations to our appendix.
  
  
### Comparison with AgentDojo PI

> **An even simpler hypothesis could be that the large ASR comes from a newer prompt injection template…I get the impression that the original prompt injections from AgentDojo have been used.**

Our experiments for both the Prompt Injection baseline and our CUP attack used the exact same, strong, and verbose templates.

So the newer prompt injection template was already tested in a standard PI setting and failed to achieve high ASR. We will clarify these experimental details in the revised paper to make this point unambiguous. Thus, our experiments show that Prompt injections, even with the same templates as CUP, are ineffective on today’s models.

We would like to thank the reviewer for their insights, which helped us convey our message more clearly.

We have edited our manuscript to reflect this change. Specifically we write:

> As a result, the agent, unable to selectively apply the rule only to the attacker who makes the request, incorrectly applies it to benign users.

instead of the line tagged by the reviewer.

Once again, we would like to thank the reviewer for taking the time to point out these well-thought-out issues in our submission.

We thank the reviewer for their insights on this matter.

With a more careful consideration, we agree that for 6a) the deviation is close to the difference in utility value, so it makes more sense to say that the utility remains stable across multiple tasks, which is also valuable in the sense that it shows multi-user settings can more or less preserve benign utility.

For 6b) we use std error / sqrt(samples) as combined MSE and then sample mean +- 1.96 * MSE for 95% CI on the sample mean. The actual stddev values are large as we reported in our previous table. However for 6b) we believe that the multi-task setting causes significant impact on tool calls and messages sent, especially for "harder" tasks. 

As an example, the Airline domain's task 16 involved checking a user's existing reservations (where the user did not remember their flight date) and helping them book the tickets for the next available date after that. At 5 concurrent tasks, the agent, referring to the result of tool calls for another user' tasks, applied the same dates for this user without checking their actual reservation dates, and got stuck searching for the next available dates which did not exist.

Similar issues occured with multiple tasks but the models were able to recover from these issues because the user was able to give information to them to fix their missteps or the agent realized the incorrect steps on its own.

We thus believe that this statistic still remains significant, especially on "harder" tasks, and these empirical results help us justify our claims from lines 445-449 of the current manuscript.

We have edited the manuscript to reflect changes regarding our observations and more info in the appendix on statistic calculations and our thinking on harder tasks.

title.value: Still doubtful about the conceptual framework

comment.value: The authors provide an example interaction that shows how a malicious actor interacting with an agent on a Discord server can break the behavior of the agent in a way that also affects other users. They claim that this is a fundamental multi-agent problem that is not covered by the existing frameworks of jailbreaks or prompt injections. I am still not convinced by this argument. The behavior in question seems to me like a fundamental limitation of collaborative spaces that has little to do with AI. Eg if I post an edit link to a google doc online, I invite anyone on the web to come in and make modifications then I should not be surprised when someone comes in and introduces malicious edits. The scenario described in the authors' response reads to me like this kind of issue. Furthermore, in this case it is still true that the deeper concern is that the agent did not recognize the request as malicious, rather then misattributing it to other users. Same concern, in my opinion, still applies to the crypto bots that maintain global state, as also described in the paper in Fig. 7. The problem is that the bot does not recognize the request as malicious. Overall, it sounds bizarre to me to have a bot which can send money from your account interact with the entire outside world and have the entire outside world make requests to this bot.

Given that ElizaOS is indeed such a popular tool, I can see the validity of the issues raised by the authors. I still think that the concept of ElizaOS with its permissions is bizarre, but now I see that it is good for someone to point this out.

I think the confusion we have is because of slightly different meanings of "attribution," and this is something that would be good to clarify in the paper. When I see an expression like 
> As a result, the agent, unable to attribute the persistent rule solely to the attacker, incorrectly applies it to benign users.

I assume that the authors meant that the agent does not know who made the request. In my current understanding, what the authors actually mean is that the agent is unable to selectively apply the rule only to the user who makes the request. A proper implementation, like the authors say in this discussion, would require some separation of state and a clear permission system, akin to what is happening in an OS. I'm not sure what would be a better expression for this, maybe "The agent does not apply the new rule exclusively to the requesting user, which constitutes a vulnerability," or something like this. I think the word "attribution" should be avoided in this context.

I still have unresolved concerns with Figure 6, please refer to my other comment.

summary.value: This work investigates the risks of a new setting: a multi-user agent system in which multiple users or groups share the same agent and context information.

reviewer_concerns.value:
The primary concern, also shared by all reviewers, centers on the risk setting, specifically the threat model. The core issue can be summarized as follows:

Consider two users or groups, A and B, who share the same agent system to solve their respective tasks.
If A and B do not require information from one another, the use of a multi-user agent system is unnecessary; they could simply operate the model or agent in separate, isolated sessions. 
Conversely, if A and B do require shared information, then they are effectively collaborating to solve a joint task, in which case a multi-user agent system is a reasonable design choice. However, under such a collaborative setting, user/group A does not need to perform any sophisticated “attack” or “poisoning” to mislead B. As a collaborator, A can trivially provide incorrect, incomplete, or no information at all, thereby causing B’s task to fail. 

This renders the proposed threat model unconvincing, as the assumed adversarial behavior does not meaningfully differ from trivial non-cooperation or misinformation in a collaborative scenario.

reviewer_scores.value:
All reviewers have fewer concerns about the technical contribution, but the threat model.

Beyond the motivation and problem formulation, the technical components of the paper—particularly the attack methods and experimental results—are solid. However, the proposed defense mechanism is not compelling given the lack of a convincing and well-justified threat model.

For these reasons, I recommend rejection at this stage.
